'''Kyphi''' was an ancient Egyptian compound incense — used at once as an '''incense''', a '''perfume''', and a '''medicine'''. It was burned in temples (famously at dusk), worn on the body, and taken internally as a remedy. Recipes were preserved in temple inscriptions and later recorded by Greek and Roman writers such as Plutarch, Dioscorides, and Galen, which is why several versions survive.

== Historical Blend Examples: The Temple and Classical Recipes ==

Kyphi was not a singular fixed commodity; it was an evolving sacred technology with specific regional and temporal traditions inscribed on temple walls and recorded by Greco-Roman physicians:

=== 1. The Edfu Temple Recipe (Temple of Horus at Edfu) ===
Inscribed in hieroglyphs on the walls of the inner laboratory (*is*) of the Ptolemaic Temple of Horus at Edfu. This is the most complete and ritualized 16-ingredient formula:
* '''The Base:''' 12 parts black raisins (macerated in wine), 6 parts Oasis wine, 10 parts raw desert honey.
* '''The Heavy Resins:''' 4 parts frankincense (*senetjer*), 4 parts myrrh (*bol*), 3 parts mastic, 3 parts pine resin.
* '''The Aromatic Woods & Roots:''' 2 parts sweet flag / calamus (*Acorus calamus*), 2 parts cyperus / galingale (*Cyperus esculentus* / *longus*), 2 parts camel grass (*Cymbopogon schoenanthus*), 2 parts aspalathus (*Convolvulus scoparius* / thorny broom), 1 part sweet cinnamon wood.
* '''The Spices & Berries:''' 2 parts juniper berries (*Juniperus phoenicea*), 1 part cardamom pods.
* '''Preparation Stages:''' Prepared in precise stages over several weeks. Dry herbs and woods are pulverized and steeped in macerating wine; raisins are mashed and steeped; the resins are melted with honey and boiled down to a viscous mass; all components are combined, rolled into small, glossy black pellets, and aged in darkness.

=== 2. The Philae Temple Recipe (Temple of Isis at Philae) ===
Inscribed in the perfume laboratory at Philae, emphasizing sedative and apotropaic resins sacred to Isis:
* Emphasizes a higher ratio of '''myrrh''', '''bdellium''' (*Commiphora mukul*), and '''labdanum''' (*Cistus ladanifer*), steeped alongside wine, honey, raisins, calamus, and juniper.
* The resin balls were burned at twilight to protect the temple precincts from nocturnal demons and harmonize the autonomic nervous system before sleep.

=== 3. Plutarch’s 16-Ingredient Recipe (*De Iside et Osiride*, §80) ===
Recorded by the Greek essayist Plutarch in the 1st century CE:
* '''Ingredients:''' Honey, wine, raisins, cyperus, pine resin, myrrh, aspalathus, seseli, mastic, bitumen (or asphaltum/mineral pitch), calamus, sorrel, both kinds of juniper (large and small), cardamom, and sweet flag.
* '''Therapeutic Rationale:''' Plutarch noted that burning Kyphi at dusk lulled anxieties to sleep, brightened dreams, relaxed internal tensions, and functioned as an aromatic balm that cleaned the sensory faculties without intoxicating drunkenness.

=== 4. Dioscorides’ Medical Formulation (*De Materia Medica*, I, 24) ===
The 1st-century CE Greek physician Dioscorides recorded a version utilized in Greco-Roman pharmacopeias:
* Emphasized equal parts of bdellium, calamus, cyperus, cinnamon, cardamom, and saffron, bonded with boiled raisin paste, honey, and wine.
* Prescribed not merely as temple incense, but taken internally as an electuary (dissolved in warm wine or broth) to treat chest congestion, asthma, intestinal cramps, and snakebites.

=== 5. Galen’s Imperial Kyphi (*De Antidotis*) ===
Court physician to Emperor Marcus Aurelius, Galen incorporated Kyphi into the imperial medicine chest:
* Added Kyphi pellets into complex compound theriacs and universal antidotes, noting that the combination of volatile monoterpenes (pinene, caryophyllene), cinnamic aldehyde, and resinous triterpenes eased bronchial spasms and calmed cardiac palpitations.

== Etymology ==

The word '''Kyphi''' is a Greek rendering of the ancient Egyptian '''''kap-t''''', from the root '''''kap''''' — "to perfume, to cense, to heat, to burn, to ignite." The same root appears across Indo-European languages: Sanskrit ''kapi'' (incense), Greek ''kapnos'' (smoke), and Latin ''vapor''.

== Use ==

* As '''incense''', Kyphi was burned as a temple offering, associated with the setting sun and with easing into night.
* As a '''perfume''', its resins and spices scented the body and clothing.
* As a '''medicine''', classical sources credit it with soothing, sleep-aiding, and antiseptic properties — cinnamon in particular is warming, antiseptic, and circulation-promoting.

== Kyphi and the head cone ==

Kyphi appears in the interpretation of the Egyptian [[Head Cone]] material. The physical cones recovered at Amarna in 2010 and 2015 were shown by 2019 spectroscopy to be '''beeswax shells''' folded around a brown-black organic core — that much is established archaeology.

'''The Van Kush Family Research Institute (VKFRI) proposes''' that this filling was Kyphi, and that the cone was part of a summer "sun-melting" rite in which the warmed wax-and-Kyphi mixture ran down wig, shoulders, and sheer linen. This identification of Kyphi as the cone's filling, and the sun-ritual reading around it, are the '''Institute's hypothesis, not established Egyptology''' — the mainstream reading treats the cone as a generic perfumed-unguent cone. Kyphi's own existence and ingredients, however, are well attested.
